children: A corporate litigator who clerked for US Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas won Senate confirmation on Thursday to serve as a federal judge in a Texas court that has become a favorite for conservative litigants challenging Democratic policies.
The Republican-led Senate voted 49-45 in favor of Dallas-based Kirkland & Ellis partner Kasdin Mitchell becoming a life-tenured judge in the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

The vote gave President Donald Trump his 55th confirmed judicial appointment of his second term, as the White House looks to fill as many court vacancies as possible before the year's end amid the looming risk that Democrats retake the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections.
Those 55 add to 234 previous appointments Trump made in his first term to the lower courts and the US Supreme Court, helping shift the judiciary's ideological balance to the right.

Mitchell will join a Texas court that is dominated by other Republican-appointed judges, which made it a popular forum for conservative litigants and business groups challenging Democratic President Joe Biden's agenda during his term.
Of the court's 10 active judges, only one was appointed by a Democrat and seven were named by Trump, including Mitchell.

A Federalist Society member in her early 40s, Mitchell served as assistant press secretary to First Lady Laura Bush before attending Yale Law School and became an appellate lawyer in the Alabama attorney general's office after graduating.

She went on to clerk for now-Chief US Circuit Judge William Pryor of the 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals before later clerking from 2016 to 2017 for Thomas, the senior member of the Supreme Court's 6-3 conservative majority.

She joined Kirkland & Ellis in 2017, where she has represented companies ranging from Meta Platforms to 3M. According to her financial disclosure report, she earned nearly $3.48 million as a partner at the firm last year.

While at Kirkland, she worked alongside now-former partner Paul Clement as counsel to the New York State Rifle & Pistol Association in a landmark US Supreme Court case that reshaped modern firearms regulation.

The Supreme Court in that 2022 case, New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, declared for the first time that the US Constitution protects an individual's right to carry a handgun in public for self-defense.
It also established a new test for assessing firearms laws, saying restrictions must be "consistent with this nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation."

Last year, the Supreme Court appointed Mitchell to brief and argue a case as a friend-of-the-court in Bowe v. United States, a case concerning a prisoner’s efforts to secure post-conviction relief, after the parties agreed with each others' positions. The court often turns to former clerks to present arguments in such cases.
